narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies eclipsing binary star systems in data from NASA's TESS satellite. When two stars orbit each other, they periodically block each other's light as seen from Earth, creating a telltale dip in brightness. TESS captures these light curves for hundreds of thousands of stars, but spotting real eclipsing binaries among the noise requires careful vetting. Star Vetter runs candidates through a multi-stage pipeline: statistical checks ensure the signal is real, cross-matching against six known variable-star catalogs eliminates known systems, and an automated pixel-level check confirms the signal comes from the intended star and not a nearby interloper. A machine learning model trained on thousands of labeled examples provides a second opinion on candidate quality, outperforming the rule-based baseline. So far, the project has confirmed 226 eclipsing binary candidates across 1.8% of the TESS sky. Each candidate is listed with its measured orbital period and eclipse depths, along with any caveats that emerged during vetting.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a system of two stars orbiting each other such that, from Earth's perspective, one star periodically passes in front of the other. Each time this happens, the total light we receive from the system dips noticeably. By studying these eclipses, astronomers can measure the orbital period and infer other properties of the stars.

faqs.question: What is a 'candidate' versus a 'confirmed' candidate?
faqs.answer: A candidate is a potential eclipsing binary detected by automated analysis of a TESS light curve. A 'confirmed' candidate on Star Vetter has passed all stages of the vetting pipeline, including an automated pixel-level check that verifies the signal comes from the intended target star and not a nearby contaminant. 'Confirmed' refers only to passing this pipeline check, not to independent scientific verification.

faqs.question: What is the machine learning screening score?
faqs.answer: Star Vetter uses a gradient boosting model trained on 2,333 labeled examples to score candidate quality. This model outperforms the rule-based baseline used to decide which candidates undergo pixel-level checking. The ML score serves as a second opinion on candidate reliability but does not itself gate which candidates are checked or determine which results are listed.

faqs.question: How is each candidate checked?
faqs.answer: After statistical vetting and cross-matching against known catalogs, each candidate undergoes an automated pixel-level check. This fully automated process examines the spatial distribution of the light-curve signal to confirm it originates from the intended target star rather than a nearby source. Candidates that pass this check are listed as confirmed.

faqs.question: What if the period looks aliased?
faqs.answer: If a candidate's measured period is ambiguous due to the spacing of observations, an automated odd/even eclipse-depth test is applied. This test compares the depths of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses to identify whether a different period explains the data better. Any caveat discovered this way is noted on the candidate's individual page.

faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each confirmed candidate includes a link to the underlying TESS light curve and its measured orbital period. You can download the data and examine the eclipses yourself using standard astronomy software. Star Vetter provides the measurements and a summary of vetting steps, but independent confirmation by other astronomers is always possible and encouraged.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed here?
faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter marks the end of this automated pipeline. The project does not perform spectroscopy, arrange follow-up observations, add candidates to official catalogs, or guide external research efforts. What candidates are listed here, along with their measured periods and eclipse depths, is the deliverable of the project itself.
